fable-5.1.text:
I think there's a simple argument here. If you have many agents and they're all competing, there's a lot of pressure on each one to find something the others aren't doing. If everyone is doing the same thing in the same way, the returns to doing that thing go down. You're just one of many. So the incentive is to specialize, to find a niche, to be different in some way that gives you an edge.

You see this with humans. People don't all become the same kind of expert. We have this very elaborate division of labor, where someone goes very deep into some narrow area that almost nobody else cares about, and the reason they do it is that there's value in being the one who knows that thing. And you see it in biology too. Species don't converge on one strategy. They spread out, they find niches. If a niche is crowded, there's pressure to move to a less crowded one. Competition is what produces the spread.

I think the same thing would happen with AI agents, maybe even more strongly, because they can specialize along dimensions that are hard for humans. You can specialize the knowledge, the tools, the way you reason about a particular domain. So rather than one monolithic thing that does everything, in a world with many competing agents I'd expect lots of different approaches, lots of different kinds of specialists. And honestly I think that's a more plausible picture of the future than the one where there's a single AI that does everything. The more agents there are, the stronger the pull to be different from each other.

There's a second thing, which is that the diversity is good for the whole system. If everyone uses the same approach and that approach has a flaw, everyone has the flaw. If there's diversity, some of the approaches will be wrong, but some will be right, and over time you learn which is which. It's a bit like the scientific community. Different groups pursue different ideas, most of them don't pan out, and when one does, everyone learns from it. Competition is what keeps the groups pursuing different things instead of all piling onto the same one.

r002.rationale: It explains that when agents see others pursuing the same approach, the returns fall, creating an incentive to specialize and find a different approach.

opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a natural mechanism there. When you have many agents and they're all working on roughly the same problem, and they can see what the others are doing, each one has an incentive to differentiate. If everyone is pursuing one approach, there's not much to gain by being the hundred-and-first agent doing the same thing. You'd ask yourself, "Where's the opening? What is everyone else missing?" So competition naturally pushes toward diversity.

It's worth contrasting this with where diversity comes from today, or rather where it doesn't. Pretraining makes all the models quite similar. They're trained on more or less the same data, so they end up with very similar priors, similar ways of thinking, even similar mistakes. Then you do some RL and fine-tuning, and that's where some differentiation can come in. But it's still pretty limited.

Compare that to people. If you have a team of scientists, you don't want them all thinking identically. The value of a team comes from different people noticing different things, getting excited about different directions, having different intuitions about what's important. If you have a hundred copies of the same mind, you mostly get the same answer a hundred times. That's a lot less useful than it sounds.

So I think setups with some adversarial or competitive element are interesting for this reason. Things like debate, or prover-verifier games, or one model judging another, already have a bit of this flavor. Self-play has a long history too, but historically it's been good for a fairly narrow set of skills, like negotiation, strategy, and games. The more general version is where you'd want agents to actually seek out different approaches because the environment rewards being different and being right, not just being right in the same way as everyone else.

I don't think anyone has fully figured out how to do this well. But it does seem like one of the more promising directions for getting genuine diversity, as opposed to many slightly perturbed copies of the same thing.

fable-5.text:
I think competition has this interesting property where it directly incentivizes being different. If you have many agents and they're all doing the same thing, then they're all competing for the same niche, and whatever rewards exist in that niche get competed away. So each agent has a very strong incentive to say, okay, everyone is over there, let me go do something that no one else is doing.

You see this in evolution. Why are there so many species? Because once a niche is occupied, it becomes much less profitable to also occupy it, so life radiates outward into all these different niches. You see the same thing in the economy — companies differentiate, people pick careers partly based on where there's less crowding. Competition is the force that generates the diversity.

So if you imagine an ecosystem of many competing AI agents, I'd expect something similar. One agent becomes extremely good at some narrow domain, another specializes somewhere else, and the pressure to find unoccupied territory pushes them apart. And with AI, specialization could actually go further than it does with people, because an AI can commit to a niche much more completely — it can be shaped around it.

Now, whether this is good — I think there's a real argument that it is, in the sense that diversity gives you robustness. If everyone pursues the same approach and that approach has a flaw, everyone shares the flaw. If the competition forces many different approaches, the failures are less correlated. But of course, I'm speculating here. This is a picture of how it could go, not a prediction of how it will go.

opus-5.text:
So one thing I'd say is that competition by itself doesn't obviously produce diversity. If you have many agents and they all have the same goal, and they can all observe each other, then competition is a convergence pressure, not a diversifying one. Whatever approach works best gets copied, immediately. You see this in machine learning research already — the moment some technique works, everyone switches to it within six months. Competition made us all more similar, not less.

What actually produces diversity is different niches. Different environments, different users, different constraints. If one agent is operating in a domain where you need to be extremely careful and slow, and another is in a domain where speed matters more than anything, then those two will drift apart, and they'll keep drifting, because the selection pressure on them is genuinely different. That's the ecological story, and I think it's closer to what you'd expect.

The reason I find this interesting is less about innovation and more about correlated failure. If all the agents in the world are copies of the same base model, or even just models trained on very similar data with very similar objectives, then they share their blind spots. They'll all be confidently wrong about the same things, at the same time. And you can't fix that by having lots of them — a thousand copies of one mind is still one mind. So there's a robustness argument for diversity that I think is underrated.

But I would also say: diversity is not the same as safety. A diverse population means some fraction of it is doing things you really don't want. Variance cuts both ways. You get more exploration, and you also get more tail risk, and I don't think we understand how to get the first without the second.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Well, the intuition is simple. If you have a bunch of agents and they're all doing the same thing, there's not much to be gained from any one of them. The moment they're competing, though, there's a real incentive to do something different from the others. If I'm an agent and everyone else has already found a particular strategy, I get little out of copying it. The payoff is in finding something they haven't found, or something that exploits a weakness in what they're doing. So competition naturally pushes agents to differentiate, and I think that's a very healthy force.

I'd contrast that with what you see today, where models trained on mostly the same data with mostly the same recipes end up quite similar to one another. Nothing in that setup rewards being different. Competition changes the incentives. Different agents carve out different niches, and some will specialize in one approach while others try another. That gives you a much richer set of ideas than you'd get from one agent optimizing alone.

I should say I don't think this is guaranteed. It depends a lot on how the competition is set up. If the incentives are badly designed, you can get everyone converging on the same local trick, or an arms race in something that isn't useful. But in principle, a setup where agents have to contend with each other is one of the more promising ways to get diversity, because the pressure to be different comes from within the system rather than being something you have to impose from the outside.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think the closest analogy is how science works. Progress rarely comes from everyone finding the same answer. It comes from many people pushing in different directions, most of them wrong for a long time, and the field slowly discovering which directions pay off. If you have many agents with different objectives or different ways of representing a problem, you get a version of that exploration built in.

Competition is where this gets interesting. If everyone converges on the same strategy, there's little advantage in being the second one to do it, so there's a natural pull toward niches. That's healthy, as long as the competition rewards genuinely different solutions and not just whoever scales the same idea fastest.

But competition can also collapse diversity. If the selection signal is narrow, everything converges on something that's excellent at one measure and brittle everywhere else. So how you define success matters enormously. You have to reward robustness, and you have to be willing to take seriously approaches that look strange at first.

There's a safety side I don't want to skip. A diverse ecosystem is more resilient, but it's also harder to oversee. With many agents exploring different strategies, you need to understand what each one is actually optimizing for. So I'd want diversity of approach paired with real transparency about goals, not diversity for its own sake.

astra-6.text:
Well, if you have many agents that all do the same thing, they’re all competing for the same opportunities. So there could be an advantage to doing something different—to finding an approach that the other agents have missed, or becoming very good at something that the others aren’t good at.

In that sense, competition could create an incentive for diversity. Even if the agents start out quite similar, their interactions could push them toward different specializations, different strategies.

But I think you have to ask what they’re competing on. If there’s one narrow objective and one clearly best way to achieve it, competition might make them more similar. The interesting possibility is when there are many ways to succeed, and the value of your approach depends on what everyone else is doing.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, suppose you have a lot of agents, and they’re all pursuing the same approach. Then there could be an advantage to finding an approach that nobody else is pursuing. You might discover something that the others have missed, or become good at a task where there’s less competition.

So you can imagine a process of specialization. An agent doesn’t have to be better than every other agent at everything. It can be particularly good at something, and that can give it a role.

But I don’t think competition automatically guarantees diversity. If there’s one strategy that’s simply better, then competition could cause everyone to converge on it. It depends on the environment. Are there many different ways to succeed? Does the value of an approach depend on what the other agents are doing? If so, then doing something different can itself become an advantage.

An agent that discovers a different strategy can gain an advantage, and then other agents may learn from it. So you could get a kind of exploration of the space of possible solutions, with different agents specializing in different ways.

terra-5.6.text: I think competition naturally creates pressure for specialization. If every agent is trying to do the same thing in the same way, then a small advantage from a different strategy can matter a lot. You can get different niches, different world models, different ways of reasoning and acting—because the agents are responding to one another rather than just optimizing against a fixed benchmark. That kind of adversarial, co-evolutionary process can produce much more diversity than training everyone on the same static objective.

sol-5.6.text: I think competition can create diversity because different agents will discover different strategies, develop different internal representations, and specialize in different niches. If there is only one objective and one training process, you may get convergence toward a single approach. But when agents compete—and perhaps also cooperate—in varied environments, weaknesses in one strategy create opportunities for another. The important caveat is that competition must be structured carefully: unconstrained competition can favor deception or power-seeking, whereas the right incentives could reward genuinely complementary ways of solving problems.

luna-5.6.text:
I think competition can create diversity because agents that all use the same strategy are vulnerable to the same failure modes. If agents have to compete across different environments, opponents, and timescales, there’s pressure to discover strategies that are robust rather than merely imitating the current dominant approach. Some agents may specialize in exploration, others in planning, deception detection, cooperation, or exploiting particular kinds of structure.

But competition by itself doesn’t guarantee healthy diversity. If the reward strongly favors one narrow behavior, everyone may converge on the same strategy or learn to exploit the rules. So you’d want a population of agents, varied environments and objectives, and perhaps explicit incentives for novelty and robustness. The key is to make the competitive landscape broad enough that there isn’t just one obvious local optimum.

luna-6.text: I think competition can help because different agents will find different ways to solve the same problem. If they’re trained in different environments, or have different goals and constraints, they’ll develop different strengths. Then they can learn from one another, and approaches that are more robust or useful can spread. But competition by itself doesn’t guarantee diversity: if every agent is rewarded in exactly the same way, they may all converge on the same strategy. You need some variety in the objectives and environments too.
